article_text:
Neon has joined with The Guardian, MK2, James Wilson and Jonathan Glazer to bring “ NAZA ” to wider audiences and expand the footprint of the Venice prize-winning documentary.

In the U.S., “NAZA” was originally released independently on Sept. 30 in 85 theaters across 30 cities, and has grossed more than $700,000. Overseas, the doc has theatrical distribution in over 50 countries.

In “NAZA,” the only documentary that played in competition in Venice, secret conversations on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night reveal the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza by the people who designed and operated them.

Popular on Variety

“NAZA” is directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, co-directors of the 2025 Oscar-winning “No Other Land.” “NAZA” won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival, premiering with a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation. It went on to screen at the New York Film Festival and win the Audience Award at the San Sebastián International Film Festival and the Critics Prize at the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival. In addition to being included on DOC NYC’s Short List, it’s nominated for three Critics Choice documentary awards.

Neon said in a statement, “Yuval and Rachel have created one of the best films of the year; it’s an extraordinary work of art and eyewitness testimony that stands alongside landmark documentaries like Laura Poitras’ “Citizenfour” and Joshua Oppenheimer’s “The Act of Killing.” At the heart of Neon’s mission is a commitment to championing the best cinema from around the world. We’re proud to join the incredible team already working on the film and help bring it to the widest audience possible.”

“NAZA” (an acronym for the Hebrew phrase for “collateral damage,” nezek agavi), is produced by The Guardian with producer James Wilson’s JW Films in association with Placeholder Films and Unseen Hand. “The Zone of Interest” director Jonathan Glazer executive produced. The deal was negotiated by MK2 Films, which boarded the film for sales prior to the Venice film festival, and Neon.

article_text:
Announcement

The School of Art at the University of Arkansas Offers Tuition-Free Graduate Programs

Applications are now open for the 2027–2028 academic year.

Graduate applications are now open at the School of Art at the University of Arkansas for the 2027-2028 academic year. Applications will be accepted through January 15, 2027.

The School of Art, housed in the Fulbright College of Arts and Sciences, has four tuition-free graduate programs and offers graduate assistantships, stipends and scholarships, as well as access to funding for fellowships, research and travel grants and residencies. The school offers over $3.5 million in student support annually, which includes scholarships, conferences, research and travel funding.

As the first graduate-level art education program offered in the state of Arkansas, the M.A. in Art Education is designed for students who are seeking to deepen their knowledge of theory and practice in art education. The program trains art educators to use interdisciplinary, collaborative teaching and research to benefit students across Arkansas and the world. Students will learn the practice of art education across a range of educational sites, such as schools, museums and communities.

The M.A. in Art History, specializing in the study of the Arts of the Americas, boasts a unique formal partnership with Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art. Graduate students have access to internship opportunities, archives, and a network of curators from across the world. The program encourages emerging scholars to reimagine what art history can be through hands-on learning, theme-based curriculum and opportunities for travel where graduate students have previously assisted faculty at statewide symposia and in curatorial projects at the Venice Biennale.

Focusing on graphic and communication design, the Master of Design program prepares designers to build a better world through design and shapes students as designers by preparing them for emerging roles and educating them on designing with accountability. Graduate students have led professional development field trips for undergraduates to local design firms and have worked on design projects with local businesses like Houndstooth Clothing and the City of Fayetteville’s Arts & Culture Division. They have traveled for research projects, working with communities abroad in Bangladesh and Italy, among other countries.

The M.F.A. in Studio Art is designed to give students the space to further hone their craft and to learn rigorous theoretical inquiry, social awareness and research. Studio Art students choose a concentration — ceramics, drawing, painting, photography, printmaking or sculpture + experimental media. Alumni have won prestigious awards such as the Guggenheim Fellowship and the National Council on Education for the Ceramic Arts Fellowship.

In 2027, the School of Art will add a new facility, the Gallery + Foundations building, which will house new galleries where students can exhibit work, and house the student-run Sugar Gallery which allows for all graduate students to enhance both arts administrative and creative practices.

Applications are open now until January 15, 2027.

Visit art.uark.edu for more information or bring your questions to our School of Art Graduate Information Session at 5:30pm (Central Time) on October 28, 2026.

Kunst is Lang is de wekelijkse podcast van Mister Motley en presentator Luuk Heezen. Heezen interviewt onze gasten zonder opsmuk of jargon over hun praktijk.

Het gesprek met Jochem Mestriner vindt plaats op 21 november, van 11:00-12:00 in de AAW Hub. Meld je hier aan om de opname bij te wonen.

Mestriners praktijk draait om het schilderen als een traag, cumulatief proces: hij bouwt oppervlakken op gedurende langdurige werksessies door middel van lagen pigment, oplosmiddelen en sporen van gebaren – materialen die chemisch gezien even vluchtig als visueel verleidelijk zijn. Het doek wordt een plek van trage bedwelming, waar datgene wat het oog aantrekt, haar tegelijkertijd verontrust. Centraal in zijn werk staat de Drosera – de zonnedauw, een plant die door kleine druppels nectar op diens bladeren insecten lokt, vangt en verteert. Mestriner past deze logica toe op het schilderij zelf: het fungeert als een ‘aantrekkingnsmachine’ die aantrekkingskracht creëert, om die vervolgens weer te consumeren. Zijn werk, dat geworteld is in de tradities van het stilleven en de sottobosco schilderkunst – en gevoed wordt door literatuur, filosofie, kunstgeschiedenis, plantkunde en entomologie – beweegt zich op het snijvlak van schoonheid en gevaar, het levende en het geconserveerde.

article_text:
Week in wildlife: a bookworm bear, an angelic spider and a bald hedgehog

This week’s best wildlife photographs from around the world

“Must you, Bob?” … a wild long-tailed macaque poses for its photo, despite a withering look from its friend, in South Aceh, Indonesia Photograph: Khairu Syukrillah/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

The story of Bukang-i, the female dusky shark trapped in a port canal in Busan, South Korea, took an unexpected turn yesterday. After many attempts, she had finally been guided out to the open sea, only to dive under the net at night and swim back into the canal again. Her persistence has won her many fans – the mayor has awarded her the official status of “shafluencer” – but observers are becoming concerned about her healthPhotograph: Kim Hong-Ji/Reuters

Red deer share a romantic moment at sunrise in Richmond Park, London, UK. The deer rut, or mating season, takes place in the autumnPhotograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty Images

Last week a black bear wandered through a library in Mammoth Lakes, California, US. The bear reportedly checked out the new releases, raided the snacks and helped itself to a jar of honey. A spokesperson from the education department said: “We can only assume the new Li-BEAR-ian was looking for a copy of Winnie-the-Pooh, published 100 years ago today!”Photograph: Mono County Free Libraries/Reuters

Flower fairy … this closeup of a jumping spider garlanded with pollen, by John Oliver Dum, won second place in the Nikon Small World photomicrography contestPhotograph: John Oliver Dum/Nikon Small World

This week saw the annual round-up of the Anchor herd of Exmoor ponies in Exmoor national park, Somerset, UK. About 140 of the ponies are gathered in to have their hooves, microchips and overall health checked by vetsPhotograph: Shutterstock

Smooth operator … say hello to Ollie, a bald hedgehog, who lives at Prickles in a Pickle wildlife sanctuary in Stoke Fleming, Devon, UK. Ollie was taken in by the charity after he was found with no spikes. Vets discovered he had ringworm and a bacterial infection that caused most of his prickles to fall out. As well as medicine, “he’s having lots of spa treatments, really, and pain relief as well,” said a veterinary surgeonPhotograph: William Dax/SWNS

A rare sighting of Chilean devil rays off Santa Catalina Island, California, US. These are the deepest-diving ray species on Earth, plunging nearly 1.9km to feed. Normally they live far out at sea; their rare appearances in coastal areas like southern California are typically driven by shifts in ocean temperaturesPhotograph: Carl Sbarounis/Airpilikia/Reuters

Pancake day … a New Zealand fur seal rests on the rocky coastline at Kaikoura, a peninsula on New Zealand’s South Island. These reliably photogenic seals are known as kekeno (“the look-arounds”) in Māori, named for their habit of checking their surroundings before slumping down and relaxingPhotograph: Sanka Vidanagama/AFP/Getty Images

Snakes on a plane … these are just a few of the 55 lizards discovered in the baggage of a man travelling to Cologne from Mexico City, along with 37 live venomous snakes, stuffed into shampoo bottles, plastic containers and balled-up socks. He claimed he had brought the animals back as a favour for a Brazilian friend, but customs officials were not convinced, and he was denied entry to GermanyPhotograph: Customs Cologne Airport/AFP/Getty Images

A cocoi heron perches on a sculpture in the pond at Praça Nossa Senhora da Paz, Rio de Janeiro, BrazilPhotograph: Bob Karp/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

An aerial drone photo of elephants roaming near a village in Preah Vihear province, Cambodia. Authorities are closely tracking the herd of six wild elephants, including a calf, after the animals moved from the Choam Ksant area towards the more densely inhabited Kulen districtPhotograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

A flock of flamingos spread their wings at Duden lake, near Konya, Turkey. Turkey’s second-largest lake has become a stark symbol of a growing water crisis, with drought and intensive groundwater use threatening its unique ecosystemPhotograph: Ozan Köse/AFP/Getty Images

“Must you, Bob?” … a wild long-tailed macaque poses for its photo, despite a withering look from its friend, while sitting on a roadside barrier along the national highway in South Aceh, Indonesia. Massive deforestation has forced these wild primates onto busy national highways, where roadside feeding by motorists alters their natural behaviour and increases the risk of plastic ingestion and vehicle collisionsPhotograph: Khairu Syukrillah/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

EXCLUSIVE: The Circle Training Initiative, dedicated to women and gender-expansive filmmakers, has unveiled the five feature film projects selected for its third Circle Fiction Orbit incubator event taking place in Montenegro this week.

They include Portuguese director and screenwriter Leonor Bettencourt Loureiro’s Por Este Arroios Acima , exploring the connection between the rapid transformation of the body, city and community building in the aftermath of a traumatic accident.

It is the director’s second fiction feature after C’est Pas la Vie en Rose, which tapped into the zeitgeist of contemporary Lisbon as longtime residents grapple with implications of gentrification. Rita de Moura Santos at Grumpy Panda Productions is producing.

Related Stories

Circle Kicks Off Inaugural Fiction Program With Nukâka Coster Waldau & Pipaluk Jørgensen Among Participants

Georgian director and screenwriter Irine Jordania is participating with Tbilisi-set Nutsa.Love revolving around the unfolding relationship between an unlikely couple. It is her second feature after Air Blue Silk which premiered at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival. She is joined by producer Elene Margvelashvili.

Watch on Deadline

The selection also features Dutch director Sabine Lubbe Bakker’s Premier Souffle , exploring whether a rebellious outsider can find her place in the world after years of isolation from her community. It is produced by Baldr Film. The director’s 2020 film Becoming Mona travelled the festival circuit.

Montenegrin director and producer Katarina Bulajić is participating with first feature project Leech , about a woman returning to her hometown who is confronted by the magnitude of betrayal. Bulajić latest short film A Special Day is currently on the festival circuit and due to screen at Germany’s FilmFestival Cottbus next week.

She is joined by screenwriter and producer Ana Vujadinovic at Montenegrin company Giggling Goat Production.

The selection also includes Polish director and screenwriter Marta Prus’ drama Soloist , exploring the elite world of ballet and reinvention of the body and soul at the end of a career and beginning of something new.

It follows Prus’ award-winning documentary Over The Limit about Russian gymnast and Olympic gold medalist Margarita Mamun. The new film is produced by Telemark.

The lineup, focused on mid-career filmmakers and teams, was selected by a three-person committee consisting of writer and producer Suzy Gillet, film scholar Jelena Mišeljić and writer and director Ivana Mladenović.

They were guided by Circle Head of Programme Biljana Tutorov – writer, director and producer of To Hold A Mountain , which is currently shortlisted for the European Film Award – and Circle Co-Head of Programme Brigid O’Shea.

The seven-day residential project development retreat is currently underway in Herceg Novi, Montenegro and runs until November 1.

It is led by award-winning producer and screenwriter Bianca Oana ( Touch Me Not , Collective , Anhell69 ).

“This is a rare opportunity for filmmakers and producers to come together, to think and exchange experiences outside the norms and the excruciating pulse of the industry,” said Oana.

“We make space to reflect not only on the films we want to make, but also on how we want to make them. Urgency and immediacy give way to listening and care. This slow time is the real time of cinema, where projects can grow into films.”

She is joined by producers Myriam Sassine ( Costa Brava Lebanon) , Dana Bunescu ( The Death of Mr Lazarescu ) and Dominique Welinski, founder of the world cinema focused Next Steps Studio taking place within the framework of Cannes Critics’ Week.

The programme also features a keynote session with Dea Kulumbegashvili and screening of her Venice Special Jury Prize-winning film April.

“Circle Fiction Orbit is our cherished space for filmmakers working to reach the next level of their careers,” said Tutorov.

“Dedicated to filmmakers, this mission informs every aspect of our methodology and framework: from the curation of mentors, experts and screenings to the location of Herceg Novi and led by Bianca Oana’s unique approach to activate their potential and find a new dynamic, all contributes to creating and environment conductive to holistic project development.”

Three projects from the first two editions have come to fruition and are travelling the festival circuit: Lex Julia by director Laura Hyppönen which will compete for Best Baltic Film in Tallinn in November; IDDA , directed by Irene Dionisio, which world in Toronto and Perla by Alexandra Makarová (Austria and Slovakia) which played in Rotterdam.

Founded in 2018, Circle was built to support women and gender-expansive filmmakers. It is co-funded by Creative Europe MEDIA and organised under the patronage of Eurimage by Wake Up Films.

EXCLUSIVE: Belgian supermodel Rose Bertram has opened up about the documentary that chronicles her professional and family life and how she has coped with her mother’s addiction issues.

Production has now wrapped on A Girl Like Rose . “After watching the film, it was as if I saw my life flash before my eyes,” she said. “I didn’t realize how intense it would be to watch it all again and have so many of the emotions and traumas I had buried for years come back to the surface.”

The film was filmed over six years. It comes from filmmaker Jonathan de Jong and his Amsterdam-based banner SUPER7EVEN Productions .

Related Stories

SUPER7EVEN & MN Media Join Forces On Doc & Factual Storytelling Studio SuperIndie

'A Girl Like Rose' Feature Doc To Go Inside The Life & Career Of Belgian Supermodel Rose Bertram

Bertram broke through as a teenager and has worked for brands including H&M, L’Oréal, AP and Sports Illustrated and has also built a profile as an influencer and creator. A Girl Like Rose takes in the glamor of model life in locations including Cannes, Ibiza and Los Angeles. The Doc follows Bertram beyond the runways and red carpets as she navigates her career and relationship with her mother, Maria, amid the impact of addiction.

Watch on Deadline

Bertram said: “The thing I’ve kept secret for so long is now, in a way, being shared with the world, something I’m incredibly proud of, but also something that feels incredibly vulnerable. It shows just how much I love my mum and, at the same time, highlights how difficult it can be to maintain that love when addiction threatens our relationship.”

She added: “As difficult as it has been to relive these memories, I hope that by sharing my story, I can help other people who have experienced similar struggles in their own lives. If my story can make even one person feel less alone or give someone the courage to speak about what they’ve been through, then opening up about my past will have been worth it.”

Bastiaan Brand serves as creative producer on the film. Bob Thole composed the score. MN Media and High Mass are handling distribution for the Netherlands and Belgium, respectively.

The feature doc will be released in 2027. Check out the first-look pics.

article_text:
A Miami art dealer received a 46-month federal prison sentence on Thursday in a long-running case centered around his efforts to sell fake Andy Warhol works.

Leslie Roberts is now facing his second prison sentence since he opened his Miami Fine Art Gallery in 1997. In 2015, he received a 22-month sentence for a case involving faked Romero Britto and Peter Max paintings. He was given three years of supervised release, but the agreement was voided in 2018, after he was accused of trying to negotiate the sale of a faked Basquiat painting, and he returned to prison.

This time around, a family claimed in a 2024 lawsuit that they had spent $6 million on Warhols that Roberts had sold them. These works featured images of people who had recurred across the Pop artist’s oeuvre: the actress Marilyn Monroe and Blondie singer Debbie Harry, among others.

But the family said that it began to doubt they possessed actual Warhols, and they noticed, upon reviewing email correspondence, that they had been messaging with email accounts that ended with @andywarholfoundation.co addresses. The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, the organization that manages the artist’s legacy, uses a .org address.

Roberts insisted that the works were real and that the the Warhol Foundation had said as much to him. But the Warhol Foundation has not had an authentication committee since 2011, the year that it disbanded amid legal pressure.

Thursday’s release about the sentencing from the Federal Bureau of Investigation referred to Roberts’s “fraudulent invoices, fabricated authentication documents, and counterfeit stamps,” and alleged that he had even undertaken efforts to make the forgeries appear genuine, placing faux identification numbers from the Warhol Foundation on the back of the works.

“He exploited the trust that collectors place in art dealers and the authenticity of the works they purchase,” Jason A. Reding Quiñones, a US attorney for the Southern District of Florida, said in a statement. “Today’s 46-month prison sentence sends a clear message: fraud is fraud, whether it happens on Wall Street or in an art gallery. Those who profit through deception will be held accountable.”

Carlos Rodriguez Melendez, who was accused of working with Roberts to sell the works, has pled guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

article_text:
Across his contributions to Film Comment and other publications, and his programming as the Curatorial Director of the Criterion Collection, Ashley Clark has established himself as one of the smartest, sharpest taste-makers in the film scene in New York and beyond—particularly through his championing of underseen films by people of color. So we were very excited by the announcement of his new book, The World of Black Film , which comes out this week. The beautifully designed volume is a historical survey of a hundred significant films made by Black filmmakers or centering Black life. It adopts a rigorously critical and curatorial approach, taking care to define what a “Black cinema” can mean, and assembling a series of titles, accompanied by deft appreciations, that capture its breadth, depth, and diversity.

Film Comment Editor Devika Girish invited Ashley on the Podcast to discuss his methods in researching and shortlisting films, titles that he discovered while writing the book, and what it meant for him to have legendary Black filmmaker Sir John Akomfrah write the book’s introduction.

article_text:
Netflix is gearing up for a Rob-Lowe-filled holiday season with the release of the actor’s documentary, “ Rob Lowe : The Outsider,” and new video episodes of his podcast, “Literally! With Rob Lowe.”

Set to release Nov. 24, “Rob Lowe: The Outsider” traces Lowe’s career from his breakout roles in “The Outsiders” and “St. Elmo’s Fire” to his Emmy-nominated performance on “The West Wing” and how he maintained his Hollywood career. The documentary is directed by Chris Smith (“Tiger King”) and executive produced by Marc Gurvitz, Jon Liebman and Zoe Rogovin. Chris Smith, Sydney Schwartz and Stacy Smith for Library Film produce.

Lowe’s podcast, “Literally! With Rob Lowe,” will be available to stream Dec. 3 in a new partnership with SiriusXM, Netflix and Lowe. More than 30 library episodes will be available on the streaming platform, where new video episodes will be released every Thursday. The actor created and hosts the podcast, also executive producing alongside Nick Liao, Adam Sachs and Jeff Ross. Team Coco’s Sean Doherty produces with associate producer Sean Calvano.

The news comes in anticipation of Netflix’s holiday comedy film “In A Holidaze,” which premieres Dec. 2 and also stars Lowe, as well as “Dance Moms” alumna Maddie Ziegler. Based on the novel by Christina Lauren, the pen name for writing partners Christina Hobbs and Lauren Billings, Ziegler plays a young woman stuck in a holiday time-loop that forces her to relive the same Christmas at her family’s cabin until she finds what brings her true happiness.

Graham Phillips and Elias Kacavas also star in the film, which is directed and written by Tiffany Paulsen. Leslie Morgenstein and Elysa Koplovitz Dutton of Alloy Entertainment produce.

article_text:
Per quasi vent’anni Schwarze Flocken (2007), il monumentale lavoro di Anselm Kiefer , è rimasto fuori dai percorsi espositivi della Collezione Würth , nonostante fosse stato acquistato nel 2008. A Künzelsau, in Germania, un edificio progettato da David Chipperfield gli offre finalmente una collocazione definitiva, pensata e costruita a partire dalle sue caratteristiche materiali e dalle sue proporzioni. Il nuovo Anselm Kiefer Pavilion , aperto al pubblico il 13 ottobre 2026, sorge nell’area del Museum Würth 2, all’interno del giardino di sculture che circonda il Carmen Würth Forum, con una struttura che occupa una superficie di 140 metri quadrati e si presenta come un volume autonomo, collocato su un leggero rialzo nella parte sud-occidentale del complesso. Lontano dall’impostazione monumentale di un museo tradizionale, l’edificio è concepito come uno spazio nel quale l’architettura si fonde in qualche modo con l’opera d’arte esposta, ma riesce – allo stesso tempo – ad orientarne la fruizione.

Realizzato tra il 2025 e il 2026 da David Chipperfield Architects Berlin , il progetto nasce da un confronto diretto con Kiefer, che ha partecipato alla definizione delle caratteristiche dell’ambiente interno stabilendone dimensioni, proporzioni, aperture e colori delle superfici. La forma dell’edificio riprende le proporzioni dell’opera, mentre il portico d’ingresso accompagna dal paesaggio esterno allo spazio espositivo, rendendo il parco da attraversare parte del percorso e integrando perfettamente la poetica di Kiefer che, spesso, affronta i temi di paesaggio e memoria nelle proprie opere.

Le pareti in calcestruzzo bocciardato riprendono alcuni elementi materici del vicino Carmen Würth Forum, anch’esso progettato dallo studio britannico, ma li rielaborano in un volume indipendente, inserito nel giardino senza assumere il ruolo di un nuovo edificio museale. Una volta entrati, ci si trova dinnanzi a un soffitto alto 13 metri con sei aperture per la luce naturale, che illumina le pareti laterali o opposte rifacendosi alle tradizionali finestre degli studi dei pittori, che necessitavano di una luce il più uniforme possibile per il loro lavoro.

Al centro del padiglione si trova Schwarze Flocken – opera che combina olio, emulsione, gommalacca, terra e rametti applicati sulla tela – che con i suoi circa sette metri di larghezza e undici metri di altezza rappresenta il lavoro di maggiori dimensioni di Kiefer conservato nella Collezione Würth e uno dei progetti più impegnativi da collocare all’interno di uno spazio espositivo La composizione è articolata inoltre in quattro sezioni sovrapposte, ciascuna del peso di circa 250 chilogrammi. L’opera era stata inizialmente destinata alla Kunsthalle Würth di Schwäbisch Hall, ma le dimensioni non ne avevano consentito l’installazione; anche l’ipotesi di collocarla nel vano di una scala su più livelli era stata accantonata. Da qui, la decisione di realizzare un edificio autonomo, le cui misure sono state definite seguendo le indicazioni dell’artista.

«È stato un grande privilegio e un onore aver partecipato, nel corso di molti anni, alla realizzazione della visione di Reinhold Würth per il polo culturale di Künzelsau», ha dichiarato David Chipperfield. «Un progetto che non soltanto testimonia il suo impegno costante a favore delle arti, ma riflette anche la sua convinzione che l’arte debba far parte della vita quotidiana e persino dell’ambiente di lavoro. Il Padiglione Anselm Kiefer prosegue in questa visione, ampliando il programma culturale che si è sviluppato in questo luogo nel corso degli anni».

Il titolo dell’opera riprende quello dell’omonima poesia di Paul Celan , poeta e traduttore rumeno naturalizzato francese. Nato in una famiglia ebraica di lingua tedesca, Celan visse la persecuzione nazista, riuscì a sfuggire ai campi di sterminio ma vide i suoi genitori deportati e uccisi in un campo di concentramento nel 1942. La sua poetica e l’esigenza di dare forma, attraverso il linguaggio, a una storia di violenza e perdita, attraversa in qualche modo anche il lavoro di Kiefer, nato nel 1945 e cresciuto nella Germania del dopoguerra.

Dall’esterno il padiglione appare come un volume compatto, caratterizzato da superfici essenziali e da una presenza materica che richiama il cemento grezzo; l’interno, invece, è attraversato dalla luce naturale e prevede travi a legno lasciate a vista. La struttura non dispone poi di un sistema attivo di climatizzazione né di impianti tradizionali di riscaldamento e ventilazione, ma si serve di pareti composte da tre strati di calcestruzzo, muratura e intonaco interno in argilla, per uno spessore complessivo di circa sessanta centimetri.

L’apertura del padiglione si accompagna alla mostra Everything That Is the Case dedicata ad Anselm Kiefer, visitabile alla Kunsthalle Würth di Schwäbisch Hall dal 16 ottobre 2026 al 3 ottobre 2027. L’esposizione riunisce circa settanta opere provenienti dalla Collezione Würth con prestiti dallo studio dell’artista, e ripercorre diverse fasi della sua produzione. Cosa succede quando un’opera non entra in un museo? In questo caso, la risposta della museografia, propone di costruire un altro museo.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: No Hands : The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company documents the extraordinary tale of the titular bike brand with Lance Armstrong serving as both an interview subject and narrator.

Armstrong tells Deadline about this rags-to-riches-to-bankruptcy tale and how things could have been different for the iconic brand if he had been on board a Schwinn as he raced the Tour de France , in turn creating a boom in the U.S. market for road bicycles.

“It doesn’t have the greatest ending for the family, but it’s an incredible American story,” he says of the feature documentary. “It’s the story of an immigrant. It’s the story of starting from scratch. It’s also the story – and I love thinking about this – of the importance of the bicycle on American culture, and I think sometimes that’s lost on people.”

Unfeatured Films founder Daniel Clarke directs the film, which comes from the people behind The Lego Brickumentary , narrated by Jason Bateman, and Loopers: The Caddie’s Long Walk , which was narrated by Bill Murray.

Watch on Deadline

“There are a few brands in the history of whatever that have really owned the category, or, said another way, have named the category,” Armstrong says of Schwinn. And the feature doc duly shows how ingrained in U.S. culture Schwinn became as it got to a point of making over a million bikes a year. “Schwinn equals bike, bike equals Schwinn,” Armstrong said of its glory years.

He got involved in No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company via Jim Packer , the Lionsgate exec who is an EP on the documentary, which uses AI to bring historical pictures and sequences to life. Deadline has a first look at the trailer (see below) as the film embarks on a festival run.

No Hands recounts how Ignaz Schwinn traveled from Germany to the U.S. and, in 1895, he and Adolph Arnold launched the iconic bike brand, setting a manufacturing base in Chicago. Different generations will get misty-eyed over various models Schwinn produced, from the humble safety bike to the Sting-Ray, which took its design cues from American muscle cars, to sleek race bikes such as the Paramount.

Armstrong, a veteran of the world’s biggest bike races, has his own memories: “I did the [1989] Junior World Champs on a Paramount, and to this day, for whatever reason, I still think that’s the best riding bike that I’ve ever ridden.”

The film shows how Schwinn was cutting edge in many ways. The brand leaned into what would now be called influencer marketing, with the likes of Roy Rogers, Frank Sinatra and Joan Crawford seen aboard their bikes. It pioneered having its own stores – nowadays the A-list bike brands have their own concept stores – and it had groundbreaking designs and detailing. Having gotten generations of people onto two wheels, it had huge influence on BMX, mountain biking and cutting-edge design, but did not capitalize on these trends as they changed the face of cycling.

Armstrong’s succinct take captures it: “They were innovative until they weren’t.”

He rode a Trek bicycle in multiple editions of the Tour de France and cycling’s other blue ribband events. As U.S. audiences saw their man in the Yellow Jersey, sales at the likes of Trek and Specialized exploded. But Schwinn had been left in their dust, filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 1992. The Schwinn brand continued under new ownership after the bankruptcy and the No Hands filmmakers said they have no relationship with the current Schwinn Bicycle Company.

“There’s a world where, somehow, they had agreed to offshore production, or got into the carbon game, and if they had done that in those early years…if that was a Schwinn instead of a Trek [I was riding], we would 100% be having a very different conversation,” Armstrong says.

Sadly for Schwinn, that was not the case, but the rise and fall story takes in how a family business became a cultural icon. No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company opens with scenes from film and TV that reference Schwinn, underlining how it became shorthand for cycling.

Director Clarke says his film “is the love letter to Schwinn that generations of kids deserve.” He adds: “The documentary feature explores Schwinn’s storied history, from the iconic Sting-Ray to its widespread influence in the worlds of BMX and mountain biking.

“Through the accounts of fans, collectors, cycling pioneers and the Schwinn family themselves, No Hands tells the story of a brand that changed cycling forever and survived through the struggles of American manufacturing, family drama, fads and business forces that ultimately led to its bankruptcy.”

Armstrong was keen to get involved. “I watch probably an unhealthy amount of documentaries, so there’s just my general interest in the category, and then obviously I had a touchpoint here, I have a lot of history with this brand.”

Having been the subject of numerous docs, this was new for Armstrong in that here, he is narrating and being interviewed, and the doc isn’t focused on him.

“I thought it was a fun thing to try. You hope the audience appreciates it. I think the film is great. I enjoyed the hell out of being a little bit involved in the process, obviously sitting for the interview, but then just getting in the studio and recording the narration.”

While No Hands is a family story, a business story, a sports story and a story about moments in history, ultimately, it taps into the simple and timeless joy of riding bicycles, with which Schwinn is synonymous. The simple premise is: you never forget your first bike.

In the film, Armstrong talks about the excitement and freedom that a first bike can bring. Decades later, the fire lit by his first steed, a brown Schwinn Mag Scrambler, still burns bright.

“It’s not lost on anybody, my history with the bicycle, with the sport, with all of the races, with the Tour, all of the things associated with it,” he says.

“Still to this day, at 55 years old, if I can wake up and go for a bike ride … and it borders on sounding a little corny, but when I talk about how that makes me feel, how that is still an escape for me, in many ways, it is like church.”

No Hands comes from Tiburon Productions and Gem Pictures in association with Brookwell McNamara Entertainment and KSQD Media, and is produced by Human Design.

article_text:
As the US midterm elections loom closer, former First Lady Hillary Clinton is turning to art for peace of mind. She is in Japan for the 37th Praemium Imperiale awards ceremony taking place on Wednesday at Meiji Kinenkan in Tokyo.

Clinton serves as US advisor to the prestigious global arts prize and on Monday posted photos on Instagram from a visit to Naoshima , one of Japan’s most well-known art islands . She posed with two of Yayoi Kusama ’s pumpkin sculptures and observed that “in a sometimes dark and chaotic world, art is an antidote to numbness and incuriosity that reminds us the work of creation is an act of resistance.”

View this post on Instagram

The former first lady joined the Praemium Imperiale in 2022 as international advisor and chair of the US nomination committee. She took over from Caroline Kennedy, former US ambassador to Japan, who served as international advisor from 2018 and stepped down in 2021, prior to her nomination as US ambassador to Australia. Clinton is the fifth US international advisor and in her role recommends candidates for the prize.

This year’s Praemium Imperiale laureates were announced on September 8, recognizing artists for their outstanding achievements and contributions to the arts. The list included American artist Jenny Holzer, British sculptor Andy Goldsworthy, American architect Daniel Libeskind, Swedish musician Herbert Blomstedt, and Australian actor Cate Blanchett. Each laureate will receive 15 million yen ($95,160), a testimonial letter, and a medal, which will be presented by Prince Hitachi, honorary patron of the Japan Art Association.

B efore Paris, there was Lagos, with its busy markets, roadside stalls and maze of disorderly streets. And then there was Rachel Ojuromi, sashaying through it all and turning the everyday into an unlikely catwalk.

For the past six months, Ojuromi has taken social media by storm, transforming the vibrant streets of Lagos into her personal runway, showcasing designs made from secondhand, thrifted clothes and scraps mostly sourced from local open-air hubs such as Yaba market.

Her childhood friend, neighbour and stylist, Debby Fasingha, puts her looks together. Filmed in Gbagada, Yaba and other parts of Lagos without disrupting traffic, the videos often draw amused stares, smiles and cheers from pedestrians, traders and drivers as she struts past.

In one video , Ojuromi turns a busy Lagos road into a runway, walking confidently through traffic with a tray of bananas balanced on her head. In another , she sits drinking tea with a teenage boy at a table outside a street-side shop, with a kettle in front of them.

The shot was inspired by a Japanese advertising campaign; she had imagined the scene but needed someone to play the tea drinker. When a passerby, curious about the filming, was told that they needed an extra, she went off and brought back her son to appear in the shot.

For Ojuromi, better known on Instagram as Give Rachel a Shot , that unexpected moment sums up the joy of shooting fashion photos in Lagos.

“There is something meaningful about knowing that a particular image or video exists because of a moment that happened at a specific time and place,” she says. “Even if somebody tries to recreate it, it will never be the same.”

That instinct for finding beauty in the everyday has helped take the 22-year-old Nigerian from filming in Lagos markets to a Chanel fashion show.

Ojuromi’s love of creativity started long before she embraced it as her digital identity. Growing up, she was surrounded by clothes because her mother sold them in local markets, but she first aspired to a career in medicine. Inspired by Gifted Hands, the autobiography of Ben Carson, an African-American doctor from Detroit, she dreamed of becoming a neurosurgeon who breaks down barriers.

But after complications with her college application, she took a year off and began exploring film-making. She eventually decided that surgery was not for her.

“I wanted to contribute something meaningful and push boundaries,” she says. “I discovered that I could pursue that ambition through creativity rather than medicine.”

The Lagos videos began with experiments in creative direction and street photography. Working with Fasingha, Ojuromi started reinterpreting global fashion collections using secondhand clothes and wardrobe finds before taking the creations to the streets.

“One of my mantras is to live within the reality of your situation,” she says. “I am not going to spend money on something I cannot afford simply because I want to create a particular look.

“We are more interested in the conversations happening around those clothes. We ask ourselves what the designer is trying to communicate through the collection. What is the central message? What is the cultural reference?”

For six months, beginning in March this year, she and her team committed themselves to publishing a new fashion video every day.

Then Chanel came calling.

Ojuromi and Fasingha had created looks inspired by the fashion house’s Métiers d’Art 2026 collection . After Chanel’s casting director, Anita Bitton, gave them the go-ahead to publish their versions , their clip caught the attention of several influential figures in fashion, including Chanel’s creative director, Matthieu Blazy.

The conversations that followed eventually took Ojuromi from Lagos to Paris, where she walked for the Chanel spring/summer 2027 show at the Grand Palais last month.

But her ambitions extend well beyond modelling. She is also a film-maker, creative director and founder and editor of the Process Africa , a platform promoting young African creatives.

Launched in 2023 following an event organised by her young artist friend Temidayo Aríṣe , it aims to address the barriers faced by young artists, designers, photographers and other creatives in Africa, particularly those who struggle to access the opportunities needed to establish themselves.

“I remember looking around [at the event] and thinking that somebody needed to tell the stories of these people,” she says.

Her aim is also based on the idea that African creativity should not have to justify itself through its geographical identity.

“I don’t want people to constantly feel the need to introduce their work as African fashion or African art, as though it belongs to a separate category,” she says. “It is fashion. It is art. It is music. It is creativity.”

Against a backdrop of profound change in our cultural and environmental reference points, PHOTO ART PARIS is launching its first edition with this aim: to position fine art photography as a central medium for interpreting the contemporary world. This exhibition brings together 13 photographers with distinctive visual styles, drawn from a variety of artistic and cultural backgrounds. Each work on display reflects a unique artistic approach, whilst contributing to a collective narrative centred on key themes: our relationship with living things, memory, territories and human interactions. Four contemporary sculptors complement this exhibition with original works, introducing a three-dimensional perspective that resonates directly with the photographic works on display. The 2026 edition is distinguished by the presence of Olivier Grunewald as artist of honour. His work, internationally recognised for its ability to reveal the aesthetic power of natural phenomena, forms the very essence of this inaugural edition and reinforces its artistic credibility. Conceived as a platform where creativity and the art market converge, PHOTO ART PARIS is aimed at a discerning audience: collectors, businesses, patrons, institutions and cultural influencers. The exhibition offers: • A selection of fine art works available for purchase • A structured curatorial itinerary designed to facilitate the interpretation and understanding of artistic approaches • Highlights: a VIP opening, meet-and-greets, talks and book signings by exhibiting artists and a number of guest artists • A catalogue presenting all the artists and works

Beyond the exhibition itself, PHOTO ART PARIS aims to establish a permanent fixture on the Parisian cultural scene, with plans for annual expansion contingent upon the success of this inaugural edition.

Practical information November 18th – 29th Venue: Galerie 24B – 24 Bis, rue Saint-Roch – 75001 Paris

Invitation-only opening

The works on display will be available for purchase, enabling collectors and art lovers to acquire original pieces and extend the experience beyond the exhibition.

article_text:
19世紀イギリスを代表する風景画家、 ジョゼフ・マロード・ウィリアム・ターナー （1775〜1851）の展覧会 「テート美術館 ターナー展──崇高の絵画、現代美術との対話」 が 国立西洋美術館 で開幕した。会期は2027年2月21日まで。

世界最大のターナー・コレクションを誇るロンドンのテート美術館の所蔵品から、ターナーの油彩画や水彩画など、80点以上を紹介する大回顧展。ターナーの作品群をテーマごとに再編し、ゆるやかな時系列に沿って紹介している。さらに、様々な現代アーティストの作品がターナーの油彩画や水彩画とともに展示される。

ここでは、編集部が気になった展覧会グッズをピックアップして紹介する。

＊チケット割引情報🎫 Tokyo Art Beatの有料会員機能「オンラインミューぽん」を使うと 「テート美術館 ターナー展──崇高の絵画、現代美術との対話」 のチケット料金が 300円OFF に！ 会員ログイン後に 展覧会ページ からご利用いただけます。詳しい使い方は こちら 。

アクセサリー

ヴェネチア・ムラーノ島の伝統的なガラス工芸、ヴェネチアンビーズを使ったアクセサリー。ターナーがヴェネチアを描いた作品をモチーフにしたネックレス、ブレスレット、ピアス、イヤリングがそろう。透き通るビーズに、モチーフとなった絵画が重ねて表されている。お気に入りの作品を身につけたい。ピアス、イヤリング各2750円（税込）、ブレスレット4840円（税込）、バングル2970円（税込）、ネックレス5390円（税込）、ネックレス4840円（税込）、ワイヤーネックレス7623円（税込）。

エコバッグ

ターナーの作品があしらわれたエコバッグ。作品群で重要なモチーフとなっている「大気」や「海」が描かれ、どんなファッションにも合わせやすい。小さく折り畳めるので、カバンに入れておきたい。2800円（税込）。

犬ぬいぐるみ

《新月――あるいは「ボートを失った、きみにフープはやらない」》に登場する2匹の白い犬と黒い犬が、ぬいぐるみチェーンになった。首元には「JMWT」のチャーム付き。愛らしい犬たちに癒される。2420円（税込）。

きかんしゃトーマス×ターナー チョコ缶

イギリス生まれの「きかんしゃトーマス」とターナー展のコラボレーション。ターナー自身がトーマスとダックをスケッチする姿がイラストで描かれている。カラフルなチョコレートが入った缶は、食べ終わったあとも小物入れなどとして使えそう。1490円（税込）。

トートバッグ

ロンドン発のグローサリー＆デリショップ「MELROSE AND MORGAN」とのコラボレーション。ターナーが1839年のある日に食べたものとしてメモに残した「BREAD AND CHEESE」の文字をあしらっている。厚めのキャンバス地に、赤いポップなロゴがかわいい。5720円（税込）。

北陸製菓 ターナービーバー

北陸のソウルフードである揚げあられ「ビーバー」とターナー展のコラボ商品。《捕鯨船エレバス号に万歳！ もう一頭獲ったぞ！》を背景に、ターナーに扮したビーバーがパッケージにあしらわれている。「白えび」味と「あおさ塩」味のアソートパックで、お土産にぴったりだ。778円（税込）。

JING TEA ティーバッグ缶

article_text:
Leave your brain at the door, lest you want your IQ pulverized, if you see Taika Waititi ’s confoundingly awful, relentlessly twee Kazuo Ishiguro adaptation, “ Klara and the Sun .” Starring Jenna Ortega as solar-powered AF (artificial friend) Klara, whose overexposure to broad, deeply stupid human feelings starts to empower her with them, it’s this year’s “ A Big Bold Beautiful Journey ” — another auteur-backed misfire and unintended preamble to director jail.

Where Ishiguro, the Nobel-winning Japanese-British author of “The Remains of the Day” and “Never Let Me Go,” writes in plaintive, precise prose grounded in ambiguous emotions, Waititi fills in the spaces with pastel-popped set design, thwacks of whimsy, and gauche slapstick comedy that undermine every already-half-hearted gesture at profundity. Take a scene where two characters run to Klara’s rescue amid a burning building, only to get shocked by an electric fence at least three times, but more, I think. Michael Giacchino’s bathetic score, layered over such a bizarrely cued pratfall, crystallizes precisely the miscalculated clash of tensions felt in every frame as the movie supposedly hurtles toward a big emotional climax. “Klara and the Sun” is pathologically allergic to sincerity, treating major existential questions as treacle — and worse, uncuriously.

This latest Dystopian Future World That Reflects Our Own is comprised of what-else-but rigidly stratified class structures, bespoke genetic engineering available only to the wealthiest, and super-sentient artificial intelligence. That would be Kara, a now-obsolete B2 model android companion. She’s human on the outside, but all conductor wires and an inky, petrol-like liquid on the inside. One bug suggests she’s ready for factory recall: Klara can’t stop standing on one leg in tree pose, a glitch in her matrix and a gag that Waititi returns to again and again to absolutely no effect other than in irritating the hell out of the audience. She spends her numbered days and ways — numbered in the sense that she’s due to be shipped back to the factory for destruction — pining for the “super-duper nourishing nourishment” of the slats of sunlight slipping through the grille separating the shop from the city center.

When the shutters come up and Store Manager (Natasha Lyonne as, I believe, herself) opens the shop, Klara and her android cohorts must strike a pose, dance-monkey-dance style, in the window to allure potential buyers to take them. But they’re already dazzled and distracted by the shiny newness of the Looksmaxxed model B3s across the street. Lucky for Klara, a very lonely, very sick girl named Josie (Mia Tharia) wants to buy her, much to the chagrin of her dismissive, martinet of a mother, Chrissie (Amy Adams, in yet another role that’s… what’s the opposite of plum ?).

Josie and her single mom live on a middle-of-nowhere farm where the biggest threat (and, apparently, the movie’s arch villain) is a self-driving crop harvester manufactured by a company called Cootings. Josie is an only child who’s been “Lifted,” meaning her genetic makeup has been altered to retrofit what must’ve been an underachieving streak into a stroke of genius. She paints masterpieces and reads the great novels, day and night, as Chrissie readies her daughter for the Atlas Brookings school of gifted children. (Though when we meet her classmates, they’re all dullards with speech affectations and severely over-swaddled, sleeping-bag-like couture.)

Klara, whose philosophical raptures treat the Sun as a living deity and who is also capable of parroting any human’s voice or temperament on command, becomes fast friends with the girl. But the Lifting procedure has stricken Josie with some sort of unspecified neurological disorder that gets activated when the duo and Josie’s friend Rick (Aran Murphy) take a joyride in Chrissie’s self-driving Buick. One minute they’re flying through the fields with mirthful abandon, the next, smash cut to the car in a tree, and Josie in a coma in bed with tubes attached. The capricious shift is whiplash-inducing, as if editors Adam Gough and Tom Eagles cleaved a sizable chunk of footage from the film . Or are Waititi and co-writer Dahvi Waller deliberately obfuscating as some kind of middle finger to the audience? Really, you’re left wondering what just happened, and every cutaway to Klara’s literally juddering first-person viewpoint (which Josie also appears to share) doesn’t help clarify any of the narrative muddlement.

Steve Buscemi plays a Dr. Frankenstein type who holds the key to unlocking whatever’s medically afoot with Josie, and to Chrissie keeping her daughter alive if the girl doesn’t make it through the next nosebleed. From there, “Klara and the Sun” devolves into a kind of kooky pas de deux between Chrissie and Klara as Josie convalesces. At one point, as a fed-up Chrissie tries to shove Klara back into the deteriorating cardboard box from whence the girl came, she barks at Klara to “upsy-daisy” and get out of the box when it won’t close. “Who’s Daisy?” Klara asks. The film’s pick-me jabs at humor are frankly, flatly unfunny and grating, twisting the film at times into a perverse, almost self-aware treatise on tweeness. But that would be giving the movie too much intellectual credit.

The New Zealand actor and filmmaker is never an artist who takes the material too seriously. See how he turned fascism into Oscar-minted farce with Best Adapted Screenplay winner “Jojo Rabbit.” Here, his clumsy, winky, affected, and self-undercutting direction can’t even work the charming Jenna Ortega to a great performance, as her Klara is flattened into a bundle of manic pixie mannerisms both physical and verbal.

Ortega’s plenty magnetic on Netflix’s “Wednesday,” but her streak of recent film roles — from Sundance’s grueling art-world satire “The Gallerist” to the disastrous Weeknd vehicle “Hurry Up Tomorrow” and A24’s busted monster franchise-nonstarter “Death of a Unicorn” — suggests her talents are being staggeringly misapplied on the big screen. (“If I Had Legs I’d Kick You” writer/director Mary Bronstein, however, is hopefully coming to the rescue with her next movie .) For a movie filled with self-driving cars and powered by artificial intelligence, this “Klara” goes nowhere but straight into the sun of disaster, and without intelligence of any kind.

Grade: D

“Klara and the Sun” opens in theaters starting Friday, October 23.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Writer Adrian Cardenas is making his directorial debut with the film In an Orderly Fashion , which just completed production in Miami with Oscar Nuñez ( The Office , The Paper ), Marlene Forte ( The Rookie , Star Trek ), Otmara Marrero (Florida Man, StartUp ), and Vivian Ruiz (Bloodline, Pain & Gain ) in lead roles.

In an Orderly Fashion follows Rafa (Nuñez), a devoted physical therapist who dreams of traveling the world in retirement. But on the first day of freedom, he’s rewarded with a terminal illness. Chaos ensues when he asks the unthinkable of his beloved nurse wife, Aida (Forte): to put him out of his misery, so long as he doesn’t know when it’s coming.

Related Stories

'The Office' Stars Win 'Who Wants To Be A Millionaire' For Planned Parenthood & Philabundance

Oscar Nuñez Joins Peacock's 'The Office' Followup Series Reprising Original Role

Marrero stars as Gabriela and Ruiz as Maria.

Watch on Deadline

“Making this movie in my hometown of Miami with Oscar, Marlene, Vivian, and Otmara was a dream,” shared Cardenas, who before taking his talents to Hollywood was a Major League Baseball player for the Chicago Cubs. “I’m grateful the script resonated with them and that they trusted me to guide them as they so skillfully navigated the tonal tightrope between dark comedy and drama. Their talent and generosity extended beyond their performances, setting the tone for a cast and crew that became family in the process.”

In an Orderly Fashion is produced by Maria Altamirano and executive produced by Heidi Stolte, Chris Stolte, Sven Voelcker, Ann Lewnes, Daniel Weiser, Sharon Greene, Nuñez and Forte. Tyler Bagley, Barker Carlock, and Derrick Nevot co-produce.

Nuñez is represented by Omnipop Talent Group and Artists & Representatives. Forte is represented by BRS/Gage and Rothman Andres Entertainment. Marrero is represented by Luber Roklin Entertainment. Cardenas is repped by Range Media Partners.
